The original Bulletin 2024-07 date of 2024-06-01 was superseded and must NOT be used. Critically, claims with dates of service before 2024-07-01 do not require PA, so the pre-period is clean and the breakpoint should be placed at 2024-07-01 (start of 2024Q3) for the pre/post utilization comparison.

findings.statement: Authoritative effective date for Eastvale's GLP-1 prior authorization requirement is 2024-07-01. Status resolved, no unresolved conflicts; source of record is the provider manual EV-MAN-2024-PH (highest authority).

A superseded earlier version set the effective date at 2024-06-01 (Provider Bulletin EV-BUL-2024-007, published 2024-05-15). It was replaced by EV-BUL-2024-011 (published 2024-06-10) and is no longer authoritative.

EV-BUL-2024-011 explicitly postpones the start to 2024-07-01 'to allow prescribers time to submit documentation,' and states that claims for GLP-1 agonists with dates of service before 2024-07-01 do not require PA — so dates of service before that date form a genuine unconstrained pre-period.
Policy scope is broad: PA is required for all GLP-1 receptor agonists in Eastvale (per bulletin), with clinical criteria in the manual.
PA approval criteria effective 2024-07-01: (1) type 2 diabetes with A1c >= 7.0 after metformin trial, OR (2) BMI >= 35 with a documented weight-related comorbidity; approvals last 12 months.

The 12-month approval duration means renewals/recertifications for the first approved cohort would fall due around 2025-07-01, a second potential inflection point distinct from the initial 2024-07-01 requirement.

arguments.confidence_reason: Effective date is resolved by the timeline tool with a clear source-authority hierarchy (provider manual over superseded bulletin) and is corroborated verbatim in two independent state documents (EV-MAN-2024-PH, EV-BUL-2024-011).
caveats: The superseded bulletin's 2024-06-01 date is a trap: using it would misplace the pre/post breakpoint by one month and, with quarterly data, shift the comparison window by a full quarter.

The corpus yielded only three EV state documents; no 2025+ amendment, repeal, or further postponement was found in any of three searches, but absence of evidence in this corpus is not proof no such document exists.
Federal passages retrieved (42 CFR 447.256, 430.12) are procedural SPA-approval rules and establish nothing about Eastvale's actual GLP-1 PA rules — do not cite them as Eastvale policy.

Nothing here shows whether the PA requirement applies to renewals vs new starts differently, or whether any carve-outs/grandfathering beyond the pre-2024-07-01 date-of-service rule exist; that would matter for interpreting a partial-month or gradual effect.

arguments.summary: Eastvale GLP-1 prescribing fell significantly and materially after the prior authorization requirement took effect on 2024-07-01: prescriptions per 1,000 member-months dropped 18.6% (12.094 pre → 9.846 post, 95% CI [-20.8%, -16.2%]), and the change is visible immediately in the first post quarter (2024Q2 12.45 → 2024Q3 9.79 per 1,000 MM, -21.4%), after which it leveled off. Total GLP-1 spending fell 17.8% ($17.45M in 2024Q2 → $14.34M in 2025Q2) and the decomposition attributes essentially all of it to utilization per member (-19.9%, 113% of the change), with enrollment flat (-0.1%) and price per prescription slightly up (+2.8%) — so the spending decline reflects less prescribing, not cheaper drugs or a smaller population. The effect is GLP-1-specific: SGLT2 (-1.3%, CI [-4.2, 1.9]) and insulin (-0.0%, CI [-2.5, 2.7]) showed no meaningful change over the same window. Verdict: significant_and_material association; causality is plausible but not proven by this pre/post design.

findings.statement: GLP-1 prescriptions per 1,000 member-months in Eastvale fell 18.6% after the 2024-07-01 prior authorization effective date (pre mean 12.094 across 2023Q3-2024Q2 vs post mean 9.846 across 2024Q3-2025Q2), 95% bootstrap CI [-20.8%, -16.2%], against a 5% materiality threshold — verdict significant_and_material.

Immediate break at the policy date: EV GLP-1 prescribing was 12.45 per 1,000 member-months in 2024Q2 and 9.79 in 2024Q3, a -21.35% change in the first post quarter; by 2025Q2 it was 9.97 per 1,000, indicating the drop was abrupt then leveled off rather than continuing to decline.
GLP-1 reimbursement per member per month fell 16.6% (pre $11.295 → post $9.423), 95% CI [-19.4%, -13.8%], significant_and_material.
Reimbursement per GLP-1 prescription rose only 2.5% (pre $933.91 → post $957.08; CI [1.0%, 4.0%]), a statistically detectable but immaterial change — unit price did not drive the spending decline.

Spending decomposition for EV GLP-1, 2024Q2 ($17,453,705.79) to 2025Q2 ($14,343,494.48), total -17.8%: enrollment -0.1% (0.8% of the change), utilization per member -19.9% (113.1% of the change), price per prescription +2.8% (-13.8% offset). The decline is a utilization effect, not a price or enrollment effect.

The decline appears GLP-1-specific rather than a general prescribing trend: over the identical pre/post window in EV, SGLT2 prescriptions per 1,000 MM changed -1.3% (CI [-4.2%, 1.9%], no_meaningful_change) and insulin changed -0.0% (CI [-2.5%, 2.7%], no_meaningful_change).

Data are adequate for the comparison: EV has final quarters 2023Q1-2025Q2 and only provisional 2025Q3-2025Q4, which were excluded; 8 suppressed product-level rows fall inside the analysis window and are excluded (not treated as zero).

Authority for the breakpoint: the GLP-1 PA requirement effective date is 2024-07-01 per the EV provider manual EV-MAN-2024-PH, confirmed by Bulletin EV-BUL-2024-011 [EV-MAN-2024-PH#p1, EV-BUL-2024-011#p1]; the superseded Bulletin EV-BUL-2024-007 date of 2024-06-01 was not used [EV-BUL-2024-007#p1].

caveats: Pre/post association only: this is a single-state before/after comparison with 4 pre and 4 post quarters and no untreated control state is used here, so it does not by itself establish that the PA requirement caused the decline.

One GLP-1 product-level row is suppressed in every quarter (8 suppressed rows in the window, E11/E7); those counts are excluded rather than zeroed, so absolute rates are modest undercounts — the direction and rough size of the change are unaffected.
2025Q3 and 2025Q4 are provisional (claims lag) and were excluded; they must not be read as a continued decline (E1, E6).

The policy's 12-month approval duration implies recertification pressure around 2025-07-01, which falls just past the final complete quarter, so any second inflection is not yet observable in final data.

A background decline cannot be fully ruled out; the flat SGLT2 and insulin series argue against a broad secular trend but a formal difference-in-differences against NL or SP would strengthen attribution.
arguments.confidence_reason: Utilization, spending, and decomposition all point the same way with tight CIs and a contemporaneous flat control-class comparison, and the effective date comes from the highest-authority source. Confidence is held at medium because the design is a single-state interrupted pre/post series with only four quarters per side, an uncontrolled counterfactual, and suppressed product rows.

findings.statement: Authoritative effective date for Northland GLP-1 coverage (glp1_coverage) is 2024-01-01, resolved from NL-SPA-2023-014 as the highest-authority current source; no superseded versions were found.

NL-SPA-2023-014 (State Plan Amendment 23-014, published 2023-11-20) amends Northland's outpatient prescription drug benefit to cover GLP-1 receptor agonists for chronic weight management, was approved by the federal Medicaid agency, and is effective January 1, 2024.

There is a conflicting effective date: the Northland Pharmacy Provider Manual, Section 7.4 (NL-MAN-2024-RX, published/effective 2024-02-01) states that weight-management coverage begins February 1, 2024. This is a lower-authority provider manual, so the SPA date controls, but the disagreement spans a full month.

Coverage criteria: GLP-1 agonists are covered for chronic weight management in adults with BMI >= 30, or BMI >= 27 with at least one weight-related comorbidity; coverage for type 2 diabetes is unchanged by the amendment.

The provider manual directs pharmacies to use the standard prior-authorization-free pathway for patients meeting the BMI criteria, so the coverage expansion is not paired with a new prior-authorization requirement.

Federal rule 42 CFR 447.256(c) provides that an approved SPA is effective no earlier than the first day of the calendar quarter in which the approvable amendment is submitted; the NL SPA was published 2023-11-20 (Q4 2023) with a 2024-01-01 effective date, which is not earlier than that quarter start and so is consistent. This federal passage is background only and does not itself establish Northland's rules.

Federal guidance FED-GUID-2023-02 states that outpatient drug utilization counts below 11 are suppressed in public files and that the two most recent quarters should be treated as provisional due to late claims, which affects how the post-period (2024+) quarters should be compared.

arguments.summary: Southport's SGLT2 PDL takes effect 2024-04-01, the first day of a quarter, so no SP quarter straddles the policy: 2023Q1–2024Q1 are fully pre-policy and 2024Q2 onwards are fully post-policy. Safe quarters are the 9 status-'final' ones (2023Q1–2023Q2, 2023Q3, 2023Q4, 2024Q1, 2024Q2, 2024Q4, 2025Q1, 2025Q2); unsafe are 2024Q3 (missing — state did not submit) and 2025Q3/2025Q4 (provisional, ~93% and ~70% claims received, which produces an artificial −25% drop). Using only safe quarters, SGLT2 rx per 1,000 member-months moved +0.7% (95% CI −1.3% to +2.8%), a no-meaningful-change verdict.

Provisional-quarter notes quantify incompleteness: 2025Q3 has ~93% of expected claims received and 2025Q4 ~70%; 2024Q3 note says 'State did not submit data for this quarter.'

The SGLT2 PDL effective date is 2024-04-01, the first day of 2024Q2, so the pre/post split falls on a quarter boundary and no SP quarter is partially exposed to the policy; 2024Q1 is the last fully pre quarter and 2024Q2 the first fully post quarter. [SP-BUL-2024-003#p1]

Suppression in SP is minor and confined to GLP1: exactly one suppressed row per reported quarter in GLP1 (11 rows total), leaving GLP1 counts slightly incomplete; SGLT2 and INSULIN have zero suppressed rows, so an SGLT2 analysis is unaffected.
Enrollment denominators exist for every reported quarter (11 quarters, member_months ~595.7k–734.5k), so per-member rates — not raw counts — are computable across the whole safe window.

Using only final quarters, SP SGLT2 prescriptions per 1,000 member-months went from a pre mean of 15.146 to a post mean of 15.258 (+0.7%, 95% CI −1.3% to +2.8%), verdict no_meaningful_change at the 5% materiality threshold; 2024Q3 excluded as missing, 0 suppressed rows in window.
SP SGLT2 spend per member per month rose +4.0% (95% CI +0.9% to +7.2%) on final quarters only — statistically significant but below the 5% materiality bar, i.e. significant_but_immaterial.

Total SP SGLT2 spending 2023Q1→2025Q1 grew +18.3%, driven mainly by enrollment (+13.1% contribution, 73.3% of the change) with utilization per member −0.6% and price per prescription +5.2% — so raw spending growth is not evidence of more care per member and counts should not be used as the outcome.

Including the provisional quarters would corrupt the comparison: SP SGLT2 rate falls from 14.71 rx/1,000mm in 2025Q2 to 14.21 in 2025Q3 (−3.5%) and to 10.51 in 2025Q4 (−28.7%); raw prescriptions drop −24.5% from 10,223 to 7,717 — an artifact of ~70% claims run-out, not behavior.

arguments.summary: Yes, but indirectly: 42 CFR 456.703(a) makes federal matching funds for covered outpatient drugs conditional on the state having a DUR program that includes prospective drug review, and 42 CFR 456.705(a)/(b) require the state plan to provide for review of drug therapy — point-of-sale or point-of-distribution, using predetermined standards — before each prescription is filled or delivered. The screening must look for seven problem types: therapeutic duplication, drug-disease contraindication, adverse drug-drug interaction, incorrect dosage, incorrect duration, drug-allergy interaction, and clinical abuse/misuse. The duty is imposed on the state (which must tell pharmacies what to do, and pharmacies must pass that on to pharmacists); the regulation does not itself say a pharmacist must withhold dispensing, and there are exemptions for nursing-facility residents and for hospital/HMO-dispensed outpatient drugs.

findings.statement: Federal Medicaid matching funds for covered outpatient drugs are conditioned on the state operating a DUR program consisting of prospective drug review, retrospective DUR and an educational program; the goal is to ensure appropriate drug therapy while permitting individualized therapy. [42-CFR-456.703(a)]

42 CFR 456.705(a) requires the state plan to provide for review of drug therapy BEFORE each prescription is filled or delivered to the beneficiary, and requires states to give pharmacies detailed information on how to comply (guidelines on counseling, profiling and documentation), which pharmacies must pass to their pharmacists. [42-CFR-456.705(a)]

456.705(b) specifies the screening is point-of-sale OR point-of-distribution review of drug therapy using predetermined standards before each prescription is filled or delivered — so the federal minimum is screening at the point of dispensing/distribution, not necessarily a pharmacist's counter check. [42-CFR-456.705(b)]

The screening must identify seven potential drug therapy problem types: (1) therapeutic duplication (two or more drugs of the same therapeutic class where combined daily dose risks an adverse result or extra cost without added benefit); (2) drug-disease contraindication; (3) adverse drug-drug interaction; (4) incorrect drug dosage (outside the daily dosage in predetermined standards); (5) incorrect duration of drug treatment; (6) drug-allergy interactions; (7) clinical abuse/misuse. [42-CFR-456.705(b), 42-CFR-456.705(b)-2]

Complementary profiling duty: the state agency must require the pharmacist to make a reasonable effort to obtain, record and maintain patient profiles (patient identifiers; significant history including disease states, known allergies and drug reactions, comprehensive medication list and devices; pharmacist comments) — this is the data the screening runs against. [42-CFR-456.705(d)]

Counseling standards are set by state law (or another method satisfactory to the state agency), not by the federal rule directly; they must address situations where the patient/caregiver is not readily available (e.g., mail or offsite delivery) and state whether the offer applies to refills, who may make the offer, etc. [42-CFR-456.705(c), 42-CFR-456.705(c)-3]

Screening must use predetermined standards; sources may be state-developed, commercial DUR vendors, or independent organizations such as USP, and source materials must be consistent with peer-reviewed literature and the AHFS-DI, USP-DI and AMA Drug Evaluations compendia with physician/pharmacist consensus resolving differences. Standards must be public and pharmacists/physicians informed of them. [42-CFR-456.703(d), 42-CFR-456.703(e), 42-CFR-456.703(f), 42-CFR-456.703(g)]

Exemptions to prospective review: drugs dispensed to residents of nursing facilities complying with part 483 drug regimen review (states may still elect to apply DUR), covered outpatient drugs dispensed by a hospital using formularies and billed at no more than purchasing cost (with 1927(j)(2) assurances), and covered outpatient drugs dispensed by HMOs. [42-CFR-456.703(b), 42-CFR-456.703(c)]

State-optional prospective safety edits exist alongside the required screening, e.g., monitoring concurrent opioid + benzodiazepine or opioid + antipsychotic prescribing, antipsychotic use in children, and fraud/abuse identification. [42-CFR-456.703(i)-2]

findings.statement: Authoritative effective date for NL GLP-1 coverage (chronic weight management) is 2024-01-01, from NL-SPA-2023-014, a state plan amendment (highest-authority current source); no superseded versions were reported.

There is a conflicting lower-authority version: Northland Pharmacy Provider Manual Section 7.4 (NL-MAN-2024-RX), published 2024-02-01, states weight-management coverage begins February 1, 2024. This conflict is disclosed, not resolved by supersession (manual is not marked superseded).

SPA 23-014 covers GLP-1 receptor agonists for chronic weight management in adults with BMI >= 30, or BMI >= 27 with at least one weight-related comorbidity; the amendment was federally approved and effective January 1, 2024 [NL-SPA-2023-014#p1].

Coverage for type 2 diabetes is unchanged by the amendment, meaning the pre-period already contains GLP-1 utilization/spending on the diabetes indication; the policy change adds only the weight-management population [NL-SPA-2023-014#p1].

The provider manual states pharmacies should use the standard prior-authorization-free pathway for patients meeting the BMI criteria, i.e., no PA gate is described for this population in either source [NL-MAN-2024-RX#p1].

Northland GLP-1 drug utilization data availability was confirmed by the team's data-availability check (state available; quarterly statuses reported), which supports pre/post quarters on both sides of the 2024 break.

caveats: Authoritative date (2024-01-01) and the manual's 2024-02-01 disagree by one month; the post-period definition should be tested both ways (2024Q1 partly affected depending on choice).
The SPA/manual describe eligibility criteria but not any utilization-management or quantity-limit edits; nothing in the retrieved passages explains per-member use changes.

results.summary: Southport's raw GLP-1 prescription counts did grow 6.2% in 2024, but enrollment rose almost identically (6.19%), so on a per-1,000-member basis GLP-1 use was essentially flat (about 11.98 vs 11.94, a 0.36% change). The formal pre/post analysis of GLP-1 prescriptions per 1,000 members found a 0.4% change (CI [-3.0, 3.9]), classified as no meaningful change. Spending decompositions attribute GLP-1 spending growth mainly to enrollment rather than increased use per member. So members did not, on a per-member basis, meaningfully use more GLP-1 drugs; the count growth appears driven by membership growth.
